farmToFood.Objective: Investigate food origin in the Raised Food Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about food origin. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.
farmToFood.Evidence: Data table plus process sequence, calculation or evidence-based explanation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Recommend one practical change that could improve quality, handling efficiency or reduce loss.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

challenges.Scenario: A school team must improve a school garden. The team asks you to solve a know the ingredient problem using evidence rather than guesswork.
challenges.Task: Define the question, collect/read relevant evidence, make at least one calculation or structured comparison, identify a limitation and justify the preferred action.
challenges.Evidence: Evidence table, calculation/graph where appropriate, decision and justification.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Fair comparison; correct units/reading; evidence supports conclusion; limitation is acknowledged.
challenges.Extension: Propose a second option and state what evidence would make you change your decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Frame and investigate a measurable question in the Geometry Garden, analyze evidence and explain a limitation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 10-15 scientific terms linked to variables, measurement, data, garden processes and evidence.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Geometry Garden; TD-211 to TD-220; PA-211 to PA-220; GM-211 to GM-220; AQ-211 to AQ-220.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-211–IL-220, FF-211–FF-220, or FSC-211–FSC-220 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-211–AQ-220; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Investigation question (10 min) -> method/safety demonstration (10 min) -> sampling/data collection (30 min) -> calculation/graph (15 min) -> conclusion/mission (10 min).

assessments.question: Define or explain one core idea related to shapes, sides and garden spaces.
Why is a fair comparison important when studying the garden bed or path?
assessments.answer: It reduces bias and supports a valid comparison.

assessments.question: What should be kept the same when comparing two conditions?
Use an appropriate tool to collect a repeatable shape or length.
Show one quality or safety check before recording the result.
Collect at least three values and calculate a useful summary such as mean, range, rate or percentage.
Graph or tabulate the result and identify the main pattern.
Identify one limitation in your investigation and explain how it could affect the result.
Recommend one management or design change based on the evidence.
Design a follow-up test that would strengthen the conclusion.
assessments.answer: Testable, safe follow-up with clear variable/metric.

ingredientLab.Objective: Investigate identity & plant part in ginger using a fair sampling method, quantitative evidence and an evidence-based explanation.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Frame a question, select comparable samples, measure the relevant property, repeat observations, summarize the data and explain the pattern and one limitation.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Question, sample IDs, data table, calculation/graph, conclusion and limitation.
ingredientLab.Questions: Is the comparison fair? What variable are you measuring? What pattern is supported by the data?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

challenges.Extension: Propose a second option and state what evidence would make you change your decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Frame and investigate a measurable question in the Grid Experiment Garden, analyze evidence and explain a limitation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 10-15 scientific terms linked to variables, measurement, data, garden processes and evidence.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Grid Experiment Garden; TD-221 to TD-230; PA-221 to PA-230; GM-221 to GM-230; AQ-221 to AQ-230.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-221–IL-230, FF-221–FF-230, or FSC-221–FSC-230 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-221–AQ-230; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Investigation question (10 min) -> method/safety demonstration (10 min) -> sampling/data collection (30 min) -> calculation/graph (15 min) -> conclusion/mission (10 min).

assessments.question: Define or explain one core idea related to treatment-control comparisons and fair testing.
Why is a fair comparison important when studying the grid cell?
assessments.answer: It reduces bias and supports a valid comparison.

assessments.question: What should be kept the same when comparing two conditions?
Use an appropriate tool to collect a repeatable treatment response.
Show one quality or safety check before recording the result.
Collect at least three values and calculate a useful summary such as mean, range, rate or percentage.
Graph or tabulate the result and identify the main pattern.
Identify one limitation in your investigation and explain how it could affect the result.
Recommend one management or design change based on the evidence.
Design a follow-up test that would strengthen the conclusion.
assessments.answer: Testable, safe follow-up with clear variable/metric.

ingredientLab.Objective: Investigate identity & plant part in turmeric using a fair sampling method, quantitative evidence and an evidence-based explanation.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Frame a question, select comparable samples, measure the relevant property, repeat observations, summarize the data and explain the pattern and one limitation.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Question, sample IDs, data table, calculation/graph, conclusion and limitation.
ingredientLab.Questions: Is the comparison fair? What variable are you measuring? What pattern is supported by the data?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Investigate food origin in the Grid Experiment Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about food origin. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.
farmToFood.Evidence: Data table plus process sequence, calculation or evidence-based explanation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Recommend one practical change that could improve quality, handling efficiency or reduce loss.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

farmToFood.Objective: Investigate safe handling in the Grid Experiment Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about safe handling. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.

challenges.Scenario: A school team must improve a harvest basket. The team asks you to solve a know the ingredient problem using evidence rather than guesswork.
challenges.Task: Define the question, collect/read relevant evidence, make at least one calculation or structured comparison, identify a limitation and justify the preferred action.
challenges.Evidence: Evidence table, calculation/graph where appropriate, decision and justification.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Fair comparison; correct units/reading; evidence supports conclusion; limitation is acknowledged.
challenges.Extension: Propose a second option and state what evidence would make you change your decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Frame and investigate a measurable question in the Keyhole Garden, analyze evidence and explain a limitation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 10-15 scientific terms linked to variables, measurement, data, garden processes and evidence.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Keyhole Garden; TD-231 to TD-240; PA-231 to PA-240; GM-231 to GM-240; AQ-231 to AQ-240.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-231–IL-240, FF-231–FF-240, or FSC-231–FSC-240 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-231–AQ-240; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Investigation question (10 min) -> method/safety demonstration (10 min) -> sampling/data collection (30 min) -> calculation/graph (15 min) -> conclusion/mission (10 min).

assessments.question: Define or explain one core idea related to access, moisture and resource flow in keyhole beds.
Why is a fair comparison important when studying the keyhole bed?
assessments.answer: It reduces bias and supports a valid comparison.

assessments.question: What should be kept the same when comparing two conditions?
Use an appropriate tool to collect a repeatable system observation.
Show one quality or safety check before recording the result.
Collect at least three values and calculate a useful summary such as mean, range, rate or percentage.
Graph or tabulate the result and identify the main pattern.
Identify one limitation in your investigation and explain how it could affect the result.
Recommend one management or design change based on the evidence.
Design a follow-up test that would strengthen the conclusion.
assessments.answer: Testable, safe follow-up with clear variable/metric.

ingredientLab.Objective: Investigate identity & plant part in pineapple using a fair sampling method, quantitative evidence and an evidence-based explanation.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Frame a question, select comparable samples, measure the relevant property, repeat observations, summarize the data and explain the pattern and one limitation.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Question, sample IDs, data table, calculation/graph, conclusion and limitation.
ingredientLab.Questions: Is the comparison fair? What variable are you measuring? What pattern is supported by the data?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Investigate food origin in the Keyhole Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about food origin. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.
farmToFood.Evidence: Data table plus process sequence, calculation or evidence-based explanation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Recommend one practical change that could improve quality, handling efficiency or reduce loss.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

challenges.Scenario: A school team must improve a ingredient display. The team asks you to solve a know the ingredient problem using evidence rather than guesswork.

challenges.Evidence: Evidence table, calculation/graph where appropriate, decision and justification.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Fair comparison; correct units/reading; evidence supports conclusion; limitation is acknowledged.
challenges.Extension: Propose a second option and state what evidence would make you change your decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Frame and investigate a measurable question in the Compost Garden, analyze evidence and explain a limitation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 10-15 scientific terms linked to variables, measurement, data, garden processes and evidence.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Compost Garden; TD-241 to TD-250; PA-241 to PA-250; GM-241 to GM-250; AQ-241 to AQ-250.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-241–IL-250, FF-241–FF-250, or FSC-241–FSC-250 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-241–AQ-250; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Investigation question (10 min) -> method/safety demonstration (10 min) -> sampling/data collection (30 min) -> calculation/graph (15 min) -> conclusion/mission (10 min).

demonstrations.setup: Define the question, samples/comparison and safe measurement method for decomposition and maturity. Check tools before class.
demonstrations.demo: Model how to observe with repeatable technique, clear units and a labeled data record.
demonstrations.ask: Is the comparison fair? What stays the same? What pattern appears? Is there an unusual value? What limitation matters?
demonstrations.observe: Check sample identity, repeat measurements, units, table quality and whether conclusions match the evidence.
demonstrations.check: Learner produces comparable data plus a calculation/graph or defensible evidence-based explanation.
demonstrations.close: Discuss pattern and limitation, state one practical implication, clean the area and assign the linked mission/journal task.

assessments.question: Define or explain one core idea related to temperature, moisture, volume and maturity.
Why is a fair comparison important when studying the compost pile?
assessments.answer: It reduces bias and supports a valid comparison.

assessments.question: What should be kept the same when comparing two conditions?
Use an appropriate tool to collect a repeatable compost indicator.
Show one quality or safety check before recording the result.
Collect at least three values and calculate a useful summary such as mean, range, rate or percentage.
Graph or tabulate the result and identify the main pattern.
Identify one limitation in your investigation and explain how it could affect the result.
Recommend one management or design change based on the evidence.
Design a follow-up test that would strengthen the conclusion.
assessments.answer: Testable, safe follow-up with clear variable/metric.

ingredientLab.Objective: Investigate identity & plant part in citrus using a fair sampling method, quantitative evidence and an evidence-based explanation.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Frame a question, select comparable samples, measure the relevant property, repeat observations, summarize the data and explain the pattern and one limitation.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Question, sample IDs, data table, calculation/graph, conclusion and limitation.
ingredientLab.Questions: Is the comparison fair? What variable are you measuring? What pattern is supported by the data?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Investigate food origin in the Compost Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about food origin. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.
farmToFood.Evidence: Data table plus process sequence, calculation or evidence-based explanation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Recommend one practical change that could improve quality, handling efficiency or reduce loss.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

farmToFood.Objective: Investigate preparation pathway in the Compost Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about preparation pathway. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.

challenges.Scenario: A school team must improve a school lunch scenario. The team asks you to solve a know the ingredient problem using evidence rather than guesswork.
challenges.Task: Define the question, collect/read relevant evidence, make at least one calculation or structured comparison, identify a limitation and justify the preferred action.
challenges.Evidence: Evidence table, calculation/graph where appropriate, decision and justification.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Fair comparison; correct units/reading; evidence supports conclusion; limitation is acknowledged.
challenges.Extension: Propose a second option and state what evidence would make you change your decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Frame and investigate a measurable question in the Gravity Drip Garden, analyze evidence and explain a limitation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 10-15 scientific terms linked to variables, measurement, data, garden processes and evidence.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Gravity Drip Garden; TD-251 to TD-260; PA-251 to PA-260; GM-251 to GM-260; AQ-251 to AQ-260.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-251–IL-260, FF-251–FF-260, or FSC-251–FSC-260 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-251–AQ-260; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Investigation question (10 min) -> method/safety demonstration (10 min) -> sampling/data collection (30 min) -> calculation/graph (15 min) -> conclusion/mission (10 min).

demonstrations.setup: Define the question, samples/comparison and safe measurement method for flow and uniformity. Check tools before class.
demonstrations.demo: Model how to observe with repeatable technique, clear units and a labeled data record.
demonstrations.ask: Is the comparison fair? What stays the same? What pattern appears? Is there an unusual value? What limitation matters?
demonstrations.observe: Check sample identity, repeat measurements, units, table quality and whether conclusions match the evidence.
demonstrations.check: Learner produces comparable data plus a calculation/graph or defensible evidence-based explanation.
demonstrations.close: Discuss pattern and limitation, state one practical implication, clean the area and assign the linked mission/journal task.

assessments.question: Define or explain one core idea related to flow rate, uniformity and applied water.
Why is a fair comparison important when studying the drip emitter?
assessments.answer: It reduces bias and supports a valid comparison.

assessments.question: What should be kept the same when comparing two conditions?
Use an appropriate tool to collect a repeatable flow rate.
Show one quality or safety check before recording the result.
Collect at least three values and calculate a useful summary such as mean, range, rate or percentage.
Graph or tabulate the result and identify the main pattern.
Identify one limitation in your investigation and explain how it could affect the result.
Recommend one management or design change based on the evidence.
Design a follow-up test that would strengthen the conclusion.
assessments.answer: Testable, safe follow-up with clear variable/metric.

ingredientLab.Objective: Investigate identity & plant part in mint using a fair sampling method, quantitative evidence and an evidence-based explanation.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Frame a question, select comparable samples, measure the relevant property, repeat observations, summarize the data and explain the pattern and one limitation.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Question, sample IDs, data table, calculation/graph, conclusion and limitation.
ingredientLab.Questions: Is the comparison fair? What variable are you measuring? What pattern is supported by the data?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Investigate food origin in the Gravity Drip Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about food origin. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.
farmToFood.Evidence: Data table plus process sequence, calculation or evidence-based explanation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Recommend one practical change that could improve quality, handling efficiency or reduce loss.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

farmToFood.Challenge: Recommend one practical change that could improve quality, handling efficiency or reduce loss.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

challenges.Scenario: A school team must improve a water station. The team asks you to solve a know the ingredient problem using evidence rather than guesswork.
challenges.Task: Define the question, collect/read relevant evidence, make at least one calculation or structured comparison, identify a limitation and justify the preferred action.
challenges.Evidence: Evidence table, calculation/graph where appropriate, decision and justification.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Fair comparison; correct units/reading; evidence supports conclusion; limitation is acknowledged.
challenges.Extension: Propose a second option and state what evidence would make you change your decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Frame and investigate a measurable question in the Vertical Garden, analyze evidence and explain a limitation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 10-15 scientific terms linked to variables, measurement, data, garden processes and evidence.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Vertical Garden; TD-261 to TD-270; PA-261 to PA-270; GM-261 to GM-270; AQ-261 to AQ-270.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-261–IL-270, FF-261–FF-270, or FSC-261–FSC-270 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-261–AQ-270; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Investigation question (10 min) -> method/safety demonstration (10 min) -> sampling/data collection (30 min) -> calculation/graph (15 min) -> conclusion/mission (10 min).

demonstrations.setup: Define the question, samples/comparison and safe measurement method for performance by vertical level. Check tools before class.
demonstrations.demo: Model how to observe with repeatable technique, clear units and a labeled data record.
demonstrations.ask: Is the comparison fair? What stays the same? What pattern appears? Is there an unusual value? What limitation matters?

demonstrations.check: Learner produces comparable data plus a calculation/graph or defensible evidence-based explanation.
demonstrations.close: Discuss pattern and limitation, state one practical implication, clean the area and assign the linked mission/journal task.

assessments.question: Define or explain one core idea related to performance across vertical levels.
Why is a fair comparison important when studying the vertical planter?
assessments.answer: It reduces bias and supports a valid comparison.

assessments.question: What should be kept the same when comparing two conditions?
Use an appropriate tool to collect a repeatable level response.
Show one quality or safety check before recording the result.
Collect at least three values and calculate a useful summary such as mean, range, rate or percentage.
Graph or tabulate the result and identify the main pattern.
Identify one limitation in your investigation and explain how it could affect the result.
Recommend one management or design change based on the evidence.
Design a follow-up test that would strengthen the conclusion.
assessments.answer: Testable, safe follow-up with clear variable/metric.

ingredientLab.Objective: Investigate identity & plant part in moringa using a fair sampling method, quantitative evidence and an evidence-based explanation.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Frame a question, select comparable samples, measure the relevant property, repeat observations, summarize the data and explain the pattern and one limitation.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Question, sample IDs, data table, calculation/graph, conclusion and limitation.
ingredientLab.Questions: Is the comparison fair? What variable are you measuring? What pattern is supported by the data?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Investigate food origin in the Vertical Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about food origin. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.
farmToFood.Evidence: Data table plus process sequence, calculation or evidence-based explanation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Recommend one practical change that could improve quality, handling efficiency or reduce loss.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Frame and investigate a measurable question in the Crop Rotation Garden, analyze evidence and explain a limitation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 10-15 scientific terms linked to variables, measurement, data, garden processes and evidence.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Crop Rotation Garden; TD-271 to TD-280; PA-271 to PA-280; GM-271 to GM-280; AQ-271 to AQ-280.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-271–IL-280, FF-271–FF-280, or FSC-271–FSC-280 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-271–AQ-280; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Investigation question (10 min) -> method/safety demonstration (10 min) -> sampling/data collection (30 min) -> calculation/graph (15 min) -> conclusion/mission (10 min).

assessments.question: Define or explain one core idea related to crop-family sequence and soil cover.
Why is a fair comparison important when studying the rotation record?
assessments.answer: It reduces bias and supports a valid comparison.

assessments.question: What should be kept the same when comparing two conditions?
Use an appropriate tool to collect a repeatable rotation interval.
Show one quality or safety check before recording the result.
Collect at least three values and calculate a useful summary such as mean, range, rate or percentage.
Graph or tabulate the result and identify the main pattern.
Identify one limitation in your investigation and explain how it could affect the result.
Recommend one management or design change based on the evidence.
Design a follow-up test that would strengthen the conclusion.
assessments.answer: Testable, safe follow-up with clear variable/metric.

ingredientLab.Objective: Investigate identity & plant part in watermelon using a fair sampling method, quantitative evidence and an evidence-based explanation.

ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Frame a question, select comparable samples, measure the relevant property, repeat observations, summarize the data and explain the pattern and one limitation.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Question, sample IDs, data table, calculation/graph, conclusion and limitation.
ingredientLab.Questions: Is the comparison fair? What variable are you measuring? What pattern is supported by the data?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Investigate food origin in the Crop Rotation Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about food origin. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.
farmToFood.Evidence: Data table plus process sequence, calculation or evidence-based explanation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Recommend one practical change that could improve quality, handling efficiency or reduce loss.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Frame and investigate a measurable question in the Water-Smart Garden, analyze evidence and explain a limitation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 10-15 scientific terms linked to variables, measurement, data, garden processes and evidence.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Water-Smart Garden; TD-281 to TD-290; PA-281 to PA-290; GM-281 to GM-290; AQ-281 to AQ-290.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-281–IL-290, FF-281–FF-290, or FSC-281–FSC-290 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-281–AQ-290; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Investigation question (10 min) -> method/safety demonstration (10 min) -> sampling/data collection (30 min) -> calculation/graph (15 min) -> conclusion/mission (10 min).

missions.evidence: infiltration, applied water, runoff or productivity evidence
missions.success: The method is repeatable, units are shown, the conclusion matches the evidence, and one limitation is identified.
missions.safety: Avoid slippery wet areas. Follow teacher instructions and school garden safety rules.
missions.agrishine: Recommend one practical improvement to the Water-Smart Garden based on your measurements.

assessments.question: Define or explain one core idea related to infiltration, irrigation and water productivity.
Why is a fair comparison important when studying the water-smart bed?
assessments.answer: It reduces bias and supports a valid comparison.

assessments.question: What should be kept the same when comparing two conditions?
Use an appropriate tool to collect a repeatable water metric.
Show one quality or safety check before recording the result.
Collect at least three values and calculate a useful summary such as mean, range, rate or percentage.
Graph or tabulate the result and identify the main pattern.
Identify one limitation in your investigation and explain how it could affect the result.
Recommend one management or design change based on the evidence.
Design a follow-up test that would strengthen the conclusion.
assessments.answer: Testable, safe follow-up with clear variable/metric.

ingredientLab.Objective: Investigate identity & plant part in tomato using a fair sampling method, quantitative evidence and an evidence-based explanation.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Frame a question, select comparable samples, measure the relevant property, repeat observations, summarize the data and explain the pattern and one limitation.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Question, sample IDs, data table, calculation/graph, conclusion and limitation.
ingredientLab.Questions: Is the comparison fair? What variable are you measuring? What pattern is supported by the data?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Investigate food origin in the Water-Smart Garden using measurable evidence and explain how production decisions affect food quantity, quality or handling.
farmToFood.Materials: Journal, labels, ruler/tape, balance where available, clean containers, tally sheet, calculator, handwashing supplies.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Frame a question about food origin. 2. Select samples. 3. Measure or classify evidence. 4. Record quantities and quality observations. 5. Trace the product through at least four farm-to-food stages. 6. Explain one risk, loss point or improvement.
farmToFood.Evidence: Data table plus process sequence, calculation or evidence-based explanation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Recommend one practical change that could improve quality, handling efficiency or reduce loss.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

challenges.Scenario: A school team must improve a food journey map. The team asks you to solve a know the ingredient problem using evidence rather than guesswork.

challenges.Evidence: Evidence table, calculation/graph where appropriate, decision and justification.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Fair comparison; correct units/reading; evidence supports conclusion; limitation is acknowledged.
challenges.Extension: Propose a second option and state what evidence would make you change your decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.

lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-291–IL-300, FF-291–FF-300, or FSC-291–FSC-300 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-291–AQ-300; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Investigation question (10 min) -> method/safety demonstration (10 min) -> sampling/data collection (30 min) -> calculation/graph (15 min) -> conclusion/mission (10 min).

assessments.question: Define or explain one core idea related to flow, pH, EC and root-zone condition.
Why is a fair comparison important when studying the soilless system?
assessments.answer: It reduces bias and supports a valid comparison.

assessments.question: What should be kept the same when comparing two conditions?
Use an appropriate tool to collect a repeatable system reading.
Show one quality or safety check before recording the result.
Collect at least three values and calculate a useful summary such as mean, range, rate or percentage.
Graph or tabulate the result and identify the main pattern.
Identify one limitation in your investigation and explain how it could affect the result.
Recommend one management or design change based on the evidence.
Design a follow-up test that would strengthen the conclusion.
assessments.answer: Testable, safe follow-up with clear variable/metric.

ingredientLab.Objective: Investigate identity & plant part in maize using a fair sampling method, quantitative evidence and an evidence-based explanation.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Frame a question, select comparable samples, measure the relevant property, repeat observations, summarize the data and explain the pattern and one limitation.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Question, sample IDs, data table, calculation/graph, conclusion and limitation.
ingredientLab.Questions: Is the comparison fair? What variable are you measuring? What pattern is supported by the data?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Conduct a structured investigation in the Production Garden, quantify a response and convert evidence into a management recommendation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 12-18 scientific and systems terms; students must use terminology precisely in method, results and recommendation.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Production Garden; TD-301 to TD-310; PA-301 to PA-310; GM-301 to GM-310; AQ-301 to AQ-310.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-301–IL-310, FF-301–FF-310, or FSC-301–FSC-310 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-301–AQ-310; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Question/hypothesis (10 min) -> protocol/QC (15 min) -> replicated data collection (35 min) -> analysis (20 min) -> management decision (10 min).

demonstrations.setup: Prepare hypothesis, variables, treatment/comparison, replicates and QC for establishment, growth and yield. Assign sample/instrument IDs.
demonstrations.demo: Demonstrate how to question according to protocol, including raw-data recording and one quality-control check.
demonstrations.ask: What is the hypothesis? Which variable is the response? Why replicate? What is the effect? What uncertainty qualifies the conclusion?
demonstrations.observe: Check protocol fidelity, traceable raw data, units, replicate handling, analysis and scientific integrity.
demonstrations.check: Student quantifies the response, identifies variation/uncertainty and makes a qualified conclusion or management recommendation.
demonstrations.close: Review abnormal readings without deleting them, connect evidence to management, secure instruments and record follow-up.

missions.title: DEFINE & TEST
missions.mission: Use scientific investigation to define a question about crop production performance. Quantify the response and defend a recommendation.
missions.evidence: establishment, growth, yield or input-use evidence
missions.success: Variables and units are defined, evidence is traceable, analysis is appropriate, and the recommendation states uncertainty.
missions.safety: Follow field-tool safety. Follow teacher instructions and school garden safety rules.
missions.agrishine: Translate the result into one management decision for the Production Garden, including the evidence that triggers the decision.

ingredientLab.Objective: Test a hypothesis about identity & plant part in hibiscus, quantify variation or change, and evaluate implications for ingredient quality or handling.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Define hypothesis and variables; label replicates; collect traceable measurements; calculate a summary/effect; graph where useful; identify uncertainty; recommend a handling or quality decision.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Hypothesis, protocol, replicate data, quantitative analysis, graph, uncertainty and recommendation.
ingredientLab.Questions: What is the response variable? How much variation is present? Does the evidence support the hypothesis? What decision follows?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Analyze food origin as a production and post-harvest problem in the Production Garden, quantify relevant evidence and justify a management decision.
farmToFood.Materials: Investigation journal, sample IDs, balance/measurement tools where available, clean containers, quality checklist, calculator.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Define the farm-to-food problem. 2. Establish sample and quality criteria. 3. Collect traceable data. 4. Quantify yield, quality class, loss or process performance as appropriate. 5. Identify a critical loss/handling point. 6. Recommend a management response.
farmToFood.Evidence: Traceable dataset, quality/loss calculation, process map and qualified recommendation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Define a measurable threshold that would trigger the recommended action.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

challenges.Task: Define criteria and variables, collect or interpret traceable data, quantify the relevant difference/loss/use, evaluate uncertainty and recommend an action with a trigger or threshold.
challenges.Evidence: Problem statement, data/calculation, evaluation, uncertainty note and management recommendation.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Traceable evidence; quantitative reasoning; explicit criteria; qualified conclusion; actionable recommendation.
challenges.Extension: Conduct a sensitivity check: identify one assumption that could reverse the decision.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Conduct a structured investigation in the Raised Systems Garden, quantify a response and convert evidence into a management recommendation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 12-18 scientific and systems terms; students must use terminology precisely in method, results and recommendation.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Raised Systems Garden; TD-311 to TD-320; PA-311 to PA-320; GM-311 to GM-320; AQ-311 to AQ-320.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-311–IL-320, FF-311–FF-320, or FSC-311–FSC-320 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-311–AQ-320; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Question/hypothesis (10 min) -> protocol/QC (15 min) -> replicated data collection (35 min) -> analysis (20 min) -> management decision (10 min).

demonstrations.setup: Prepare hypothesis, variables, treatment/comparison, replicates and QC for raised-system performance. Assign sample/instrument IDs.
demonstrations.demo: Demonstrate how to question according to protocol, including raw-data recording and one quality-control check.
demonstrations.ask: What is the hypothesis? Which variable is the response? Why replicate? What is the effect? What uncertainty qualifies the conclusion?
demonstrations.observe: Check protocol fidelity, traceable raw data, units, replicate handling, analysis and scientific integrity.
demonstrations.check: Student quantifies the response, identifies variation/uncertainty and makes a qualified conclusion or management recommendation.
demonstrations.close: Review abnormal readings without deleting them, connect evidence to management, secure instruments and record follow-up.

ingredientLab.Objective: Test a hypothesis about identity & plant part in ginger, quantify variation or change, and evaluate implications for ingredient quality or handling.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Define hypothesis and variables; label replicates; collect traceable measurements; calculate a summary/effect; graph where useful; identify uncertainty; recommend a handling or quality decision.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Hypothesis, protocol, replicate data, quantitative analysis, graph, uncertainty and recommendation.
ingredientLab.Questions: What is the response variable? How much variation is present? Does the evidence support the hypothesis? What decision follows?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Analyze food origin as a production and post-harvest problem in the Raised Systems Garden, quantify relevant evidence and justify a management decision.
farmToFood.Materials: Investigation journal, sample IDs, balance/measurement tools where available, clean containers, quality checklist, calculator.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Define the farm-to-food problem. 2. Establish sample and quality criteria. 3. Collect traceable data. 4. Quantify yield, quality class, loss or process performance as appropriate. 5. Identify a critical loss/handling point. 6. Recommend a management response.
farmToFood.Evidence: Traceable dataset, quality/loss calculation, process map and qualified recommendation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Define a measurable threshold that would trigger the recommended action.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

farmToFood.Steps: 1. Define the farm-to-food problem. 2. Establish sample and quality criteria. 3. Collect traceable data. 4. Quantify yield, quality class, loss or process performance as appropriate. 5. Identify a critical loss/handling point. 6. Recommend a management response.
farmToFood.Evidence: Traceable dataset, quality/loss calculation, process map and qualified recommendation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Define a measurable threshold that would trigger the recommended action.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

challenges.Scenario: The school is reviewing a classroom food table. You are assigned a know the ingredient problem that requires a defensible management decision.
challenges.Task: Define criteria and variables, collect or interpret traceable data, quantify the relevant difference/loss/use, evaluate uncertainty and recommend an action with a trigger or threshold.
challenges.Evidence: Problem statement, data/calculation, evaluation, uncertainty note and management recommendation.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Traceable evidence; quantitative reasoning; explicit criteria; qualified conclusion; actionable recommendation.
challenges.Extension: Conduct a sensitivity check: identify one assumption that could reverse the decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Conduct a structured investigation in the Grid Experiment Garden, quantify a response and convert evidence into a management recommendation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 12-18 scientific and systems terms; students must use terminology precisely in method, results and recommendation.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Grid Experiment Garden; TD-321 to TD-330; PA-321 to PA-330; GM-321 to GM-330; AQ-321 to AQ-330.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-321–IL-330, FF-321–FF-330, or FSC-321–FSC-330 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-321–AQ-330; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Question/hypothesis (10 min) -> protocol/QC (15 min) -> replicated data collection (35 min) -> analysis (20 min) -> management decision (10 min).

Why are replication and traceable records important?

Perform one data-quality check appropriate to the measurement.
Analyze replicate data using an appropriate summary and quantify variation.
Use a graph/table to compare conditions and identify the direction and magnitude of an effect.
Diagnose one plausible cause of an abnormal result and state what evidence would confirm it.
Write a qualified conclusion that includes uncertainty or a limitation.
assessments.answer: Conclusion matches data and qualifies certainty.

assessments.question: Recommend a management decision and define the evidence threshold that would trigger it.

ingredientLab.Objective: Test a hypothesis about identity & plant part in turmeric, quantify variation or change, and evaluate implications for ingredient quality or handling.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Define hypothesis and variables; label replicates; collect traceable measurements; calculate a summary/effect; graph where useful; identify uncertainty; recommend a handling or quality decision.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Hypothesis, protocol, replicate data, quantitative analysis, graph, uncertainty and recommendation.
ingredientLab.Questions: What is the response variable? How much variation is present? Does the evidence support the hypothesis? What decision follows?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Analyze food origin as a production and post-harvest problem in the Grid Experiment Garden, quantify relevant evidence and justify a management decision.
farmToFood.Materials: Investigation journal, sample IDs, balance/measurement tools where available, clean containers, quality checklist, calculator.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Define the farm-to-food problem. 2. Establish sample and quality criteria. 3. Collect traceable data. 4. Quantify yield, quality class, loss or process performance as appropriate. 5. Identify a critical loss/handling point. 6. Recommend a management response.
farmToFood.Evidence: Traceable dataset, quality/loss calculation, process map and qualified recommendation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Define a measurable threshold that would trigger the recommended action.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

challenges.Scenario: The school is reviewing a harvest basket. You are assigned a know the ingredient problem that requires a defensible management decision.
challenges.Task: Define criteria and variables, collect or interpret traceable data, quantify the relevant difference/loss/use, evaluate uncertainty and recommend an action with a trigger or threshold.
challenges.Evidence: Problem statement, data/calculation, evaluation, uncertainty note and management recommendation.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Traceable evidence; quantitative reasoning; explicit criteria; qualified conclusion; actionable recommendation.
challenges.Extension: Conduct a sensitivity check: identify one assumption that could reverse the decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Conduct a structured investigation in the Crop Rotation Garden, quantify a response and convert evidence into a management recommendation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 12-18 scientific and systems terms; students must use terminology precisely in method, results and recommendation.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Crop Rotation Garden; TD-331 to TD-340; PA-331 to PA-340; GM-331 to GM-340; AQ-331 to AQ-340.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-331–IL-340, FF-331–FF-340, or FSC-331–FSC-340 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-331–AQ-340; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Question/hypothesis (10 min) -> protocol/QC (15 min) -> replicated data collection (35 min) -> analysis (20 min) -> management decision (10 min).

ingredientLab.Objective: Test a hypothesis about identity & plant part in pineapple, quantify variation or change, and evaluate implications for ingredient quality or handling.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Define hypothesis and variables; label replicates; collect traceable measurements; calculate a summary/effect; graph where useful; identify uncertainty; recommend a handling or quality decision.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Hypothesis, protocol, replicate data, quantitative analysis, graph, uncertainty and recommendation.
ingredientLab.Questions: What is the response variable? How much variation is present? Does the evidence support the hypothesis? What decision follows?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Conduct a structured investigation in the Intercropping Garden, quantify a response and convert evidence into a management recommendation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 12-18 scientific and systems terms; students must use terminology precisely in method, results and recommendation.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Intercropping Garden; TD-341 to TD-350; PA-341 to PA-350; GM-341 to GM-350; AQ-341 to AQ-350.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-341–IL-350, FF-341–FF-350, or FSC-341–FSC-350 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-341–AQ-350; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Question/hypothesis (10 min) -> protocol/QC (15 min) -> replicated data collection (35 min) -> analysis (20 min) -> management decision (10 min).

demonstrations.setup: Prepare hypothesis, variables, treatment/comparison, replicates and QC for component crops and land-use efficiency. Assign sample/instrument IDs.
demonstrations.demo: Demonstrate how to question according to protocol, including raw-data recording and one quality-control check.
demonstrations.ask: What is the hypothesis? Which variable is the response? Why replicate? What is the effect? What uncertainty qualifies the conclusion?
demonstrations.observe: Check protocol fidelity, traceable raw data, units, replicate handling, analysis and scientific integrity.
demonstrations.check: Student quantifies the response, identifies variation/uncertainty and makes a qualified conclusion or management recommendation.
demonstrations.close: Review abnormal readings without deleting them, connect evidence to management, secure instruments and record follow-up.

missions.evidence: density, canopy, component yield or LER evidence

ingredientLab.Objective: Test a hypothesis about identity & plant part in citrus, quantify variation or change, and evaluate implications for ingredient quality or handling.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Define hypothesis and variables; label replicates; collect traceable measurements; calculate a summary/effect; graph where useful; identify uncertainty; recommend a handling or quality decision.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Hypothesis, protocol, replicate data, quantitative analysis, graph, uncertainty and recommendation.
ingredientLab.Questions: What is the response variable? How much variation is present? Does the evidence support the hypothesis? What decision follows?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Analyze food origin as a production and post-harvest problem in the Intercropping Garden, quantify relevant evidence and justify a management decision.
farmToFood.Materials: Investigation journal, sample IDs, balance/measurement tools where available, clean containers, quality checklist, calculator.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Define the farm-to-food problem. 2. Establish sample and quality criteria. 3. Collect traceable data. 4. Quantify yield, quality class, loss or process performance as appropriate. 5. Identify a critical loss/handling point. 6. Recommend a management response.
farmToFood.Evidence: Traceable dataset, quality/loss calculation, process map and qualified recommendation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Define a measurable threshold that would trigger the recommended action.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

passport.verification: Teacher verifies when evidence is sufficient and safe practice is demonstrated.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Conduct a structured investigation in the Water-Smart Garden, quantify a response and convert evidence into a management recommendation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 12-18 scientific and systems terms; students must use terminology precisely in method, results and recommendation.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Water-Smart Garden; TD-351 to TD-360; PA-351 to PA-360; GM-351 to GM-360; AQ-351 to AQ-360.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-351–IL-360, FF-351–FF-360, or FSC-351–FSC-360 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-351–AQ-360; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Question/hypothesis (10 min) -> protocol/QC (15 min) -> replicated data collection (35 min) -> analysis (20 min) -> management decision (10 min).

demonstrations.setup: Prepare hypothesis, variables, treatment/comparison, replicates and QC for water movement and productivity. Assign sample/instrument IDs.
demonstrations.demo: Demonstrate how to question according to protocol, including raw-data recording and one quality-control check.
demonstrations.ask: What is the hypothesis? Which variable is the response? Why replicate? What is the effect? What uncertainty qualifies the conclusion?
demonstrations.observe: Check protocol fidelity, traceable raw data, units, replicate handling, analysis and scientific integrity.
demonstrations.check: Student quantifies the response, identifies variation/uncertainty and makes a qualified conclusion or management recommendation.
demonstrations.close: Review abnormal readings without deleting them, connect evidence to management, secure instruments and record follow-up.

ingredientLab.Objective: Test a hypothesis about identity & plant part in mint, quantify variation or change, and evaluate implications for ingredient quality or handling.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Define hypothesis and variables; label replicates; collect traceable measurements; calculate a summary/effect; graph where useful; identify uncertainty; recommend a handling or quality decision.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Hypothesis, protocol, replicate data, quantitative analysis, graph, uncertainty and recommendation.
ingredientLab.Questions: What is the response variable? How much variation is present? Does the evidence support the hypothesis? What decision follows?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Analyze food origin as a production and post-harvest problem in the Water-Smart Garden, quantify relevant evidence and justify a management decision.
farmToFood.Materials: Investigation journal, sample IDs, balance/measurement tools where available, clean containers, quality checklist, calculator.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Define the farm-to-food problem. 2. Establish sample and quality criteria. 3. Collect traceable data. 4. Quantify yield, quality class, loss or process performance as appropriate. 5. Identify a critical loss/handling point. 6. Recommend a management response.
farmToFood.Evidence: Traceable dataset, quality/loss calculation, process map and qualified recommendation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Define a measurable threshold that would trigger the recommended action.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

lesson.Learning_Objective: Conduct a structured investigation in the Compost & Soil Garden, quantify a response and convert evidence into a management recommendation.
lesson.Vocabulary: 12-18 scientific and systems terms; students must use terminology precisely in method, results and recommendation.
lesson.Resource_Links: Flashcards for Compost & Soil Garden; TD-361 to TD-370; PA-361 to PA-370; GM-361 to GM-370; AQ-361 to AQ-370.
lesson.Integrated_Extension: Select one IL-361–IL-370, FF-361–FF-370, or FSC-361–FSC-370 activity where it fits the week's garden evidence.
lesson.Assessment: Use observation plus AQ-361–AQ-370; record practical, data/investigation and mission problem-solving evidence in the Food Smart Passport.
lesson.Suggested_Flow: Question/hypothesis (10 min) -> protocol/QC (15 min) -> replicated data collection (35 min) -> analysis (20 min) -> management decision (10 min).

ingredientLab.Objective: Test a hypothesis about identity & plant part in moringa, quantify variation or change, and evaluate implications for ingredient quality or handling.
ingredientLab.Materials: Clean ingredient samples or images, labels, observation sheet/journal, ruler and balance where appropriate, clean trays/containers, handwashing supplies.
ingredientLab.DIY: Use locally available produce, paper labels, clean food-grade reused containers, handmade measuring grids and simple classroom balances where suitable.
ingredientLab.Method: Define hypothesis and variables; label replicates; collect traceable measurements; calculate a summary/effect; graph where useful; identify uncertainty; recommend a handling or quality decision.
ingredientLab.Evidence: Hypothesis, protocol, replicate data, quantitative analysis, graph, uncertainty and recommendation.
ingredientLab.Questions: What is the response variable? How much variation is present? Does the evidence support the hypothesis? What decision follows?
ingredientLab.Safety: No tasting is required. Use clean teacher-approved samples. Wash hands before and after handling. Teachers alone control knives, graters, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery. Do not conduct microbial culture or unsafe food-storage experiments.

farmToFood.Objective: Analyze food origin as a production and post-harvest problem in the Compost & Soil Garden, quantify relevant evidence and justify a management decision.
farmToFood.Materials: Investigation journal, sample IDs, balance/measurement tools where available, clean containers, quality checklist, calculator.
farmToFood.DIY: Use locally available baskets, clean reused food-grade containers, handmade labels, paper process cards and simple balances/measuring vessels where suitable.
farmToFood.Steps: 1. Define the farm-to-food problem. 2. Establish sample and quality criteria. 3. Collect traceable data. 4. Quantify yield, quality class, loss or process performance as appropriate. 5. Identify a critical loss/handling point. 6. Recommend a management response.
farmToFood.Evidence: Traceable dataset, quality/loss calculation, process map and qualified recommendation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Define a measurable threshold that would trigger the recommended action.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

farmToFood.Steps: 1. Define the farm-to-food problem. 2. Establish sample and quality criteria. 3. Collect traceable data. 4. Quantify yield, quality class, loss or process performance as appropriate. 5. Identify a critical loss/handling point. 6. Recommend a management response.
farmToFood.Evidence: Traceable dataset, quality/loss calculation, process map and qualified recommendation.
farmToFood.Challenge: Define a measurable threshold that would trigger the recommended action.
farmToFood.Safety: No tasting unless the school has separately approved a supervised food activity. Wash hands before and after handling produce. Use only clean, teacher-approved samples and containers. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and any processing machinery.

challenges.Evidence: Problem statement, data/calculation, evaluation, uncertainty note and management recommendation.
challenges.Success_Criteria: Traceable evidence; quantitative reasoning; explicit criteria; qualified conclusion; actionable recommendation.
challenges.Extension: Conduct a sensitivity check: identify one assumption that could reverse the decision.
challenges.Safety: Use only teacher-approved materials. No tasting is required. Follow school rules for food handling, allergies, handwashing and sanitation. Teachers control knives, heat, electrical equipment, chemicals and processing machinery.
